To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the recruitment principle dominates the simple MUL-RT and that both recruitment and selection principles are involved in choice MUL- RT.
the overall processing complexity is determined by a combination of recruitment complexity (number of recruited limbs) and selection complexity (nature of the recruitment).
the overall complexity of a movement is the result of the combination of recruitment and selection processes, and that the latter is mainly governed by the nature of the movement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relative contribution of selection and recruitment to the overall complexity of a multilimb task.
the complexity of the motor system and provides a method for quantifying the recruitment and selection principles in multilimb movements.
the study of the motor system in terms of recruitment and selection of limbs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the recruitment principle is the dominant principle for processing complexity in simple multilimb tasks whereas selection and recruitment principles contribute equally to the overall complexity of choice tasks.

recruitment complexity is mainly driven by the number of limbs recruited, while selection complexity is mainly driven, not only by the number of recruited limbs, but also by the nature of the coordination.
recruitment complexity decreases as the number of limbs involved increases and selection complexity increases as the number of homologous limbs involved decreases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selection complexity is a constant, independent of the number of recruited limbs, whereas recruitment complexity is a function of the number of limbs recruited and the coordination of the limbs.
the recruitment and selection principles respectively determine performance in simple and choice tasks.
selection and facilitation processes are more important than recruitment and inhibition processes in explaining the overall processing complexity in choice MUL- RT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
selection processes are not negligible and that they can be dissociated from recruitment processes in a MUL-RT paradigm.
selection complexity is a major determinant of processing complexity in choice MUL- RT, and thus should be taken into account to better understand motor control and motor learning.
recruitment and selection complexity are both involved in choice RT, and thus should both be taken into account in the study of complex motor tasks.
